message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Primary purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Parallel graphics rendering – originally for rasterizing images, now also used for massively parallel compute tasks. |
| **Core count** | Few cores (typically 2–32 on consumer devices). | Hundreds or thousands of smaller cores. |
| **Core design** | Complex, high‑performance cores with deep pipelines, large caches, branch prediction, and sophisticated control logic. | Simpler, lightweight cores optimized for throughput; each core does less work individually but many can run simultaneously. |
| **Instruction set** | Rich instruction set (x86, ARM, etc.) with support for complex operations, branching, and varied data types. | Limited instruction set focused on SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) operations; great for vector math. |
| **Clock speed** | Higher clock speeds (often >3 GHz) because fewer cores and more complex logic. | Lower clock speeds (often <1 GHz) because many cores share resources. |
| **Memory hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, tight memory bandwidth per core. | Smaller per‑core caches; relies on high‑bandwidth memory (HBM, GDDR) shared across many cores. |
| **Parallelism** | Mostly serial or low‑degree parallelism (multithreading, SIMD within a core). | Massive data‑parallelism – thousands of threads can execute the same instruction on different data. |
| **Typical workloads** | Control flow heavy tasks: OS kernel, database queries, web servers, general application logic. | Data‑parallel tasks: image/video processing, machine learning inference/training, scientific simulations, cryptocurrency mining. |
| **Energy efficiency** | Optimized for performance per watt on a few cores; power scales with number of active cores. | Optimized for throughput per watt on many cores; power scales with workload density. |
| **Programming model** | Traditional imperative programming, multithreading, async/await. | SIMD, data‑parallel kernels (CUDA, OpenCL, Vulkan compute, Metal, DirectCompute). |

### Why the difference matters

* **Latency vs. Throughput** – CPUs excel at low latency for single tasks; GPUs excel at high throughput for many similar tasks.
* **Branching** – CPUs handle divergent branches efficiently; GPUs suffer when threads diverge because they execute in lockstep.
* **Precision & Types** – CPUs support full integer, floating‑point, and complex data types; GPUs historically favored floating‑point and vector types, though modern GPUs now support mixed precision and integer ops too.

In practice, most modern systems use both: the CPU handles control flow and orchestration, while the GPU accelerates compute‑heavy, parallelizable parts of an application. This synergy is why GPUs have become popular for AI training, scientific computing, and even general‑purpose GPU computing (GPGPU).
